Added by the leader after the card was filed, and it changes the deliverable: the
chart must not be a static picture. New opens and new dones must update it as they
happen, and it must be readable by a machine, because an orchestration session is
coming that will monitor it and adjust the plan from it.

So T-0217 has two halves:

1. The human view (as filed): 10-minute buckets of opened vs done, in hours, on
   the reports pane, auto-updating with no click.

2. A machine interface, which is the part the orchestrator consumes:
   `GET /api/flow?bucket=10m&window=24h&provenance=recorded` returning
       { generated_at, revision, bucket: "10m", window: "24h",
         buckets: [ { start, opened, done, hours_opened, hours_done } ],
         idle_gap: { from, to, minutes } | null,
         sources: { done_series: "store events" | "plan seeds" } }
   Rules that make it usable rather than merely present:
     - `revision` names the store hash the series was computed from, so a
       consumer can tell a refetch that returned the same numbers from one that
       returned different ones.
     - `sources` is required. Today the done series reads 2 while 44 items claim
       done, because the rest inherit it from plan seeds (see the card body). A
       consumer must be able to see which authority produced a number.
     - `provenance` filters import bursts. The 33 items in the 07:10 bucket are my
       bulk recording of the plan, not work.
     - No auth beyond the same viewer rule the dashboard already uses; the viewer
       is taken from the request, never from a query parameter a client supplies.
     - Cheap enough to poll every 10s: it folds the store's events, it does not
       re-render the board.

3. A change signal, so the orchestrator does not have to poll to be timely:
   `aim wait --as <orchestrator> --channel <ch>` already blocks today, and the
   board's digest poll already exists. Whichever is chosen, state it in the help
   page and in the endpoint doc — a monitoring interface nobody documents is a
   monitoring interface that will be polled every second.

Acceptance, restated: a second process can compute "is the pipeline saturated"
from `/api/flow` alone, without scraping the HTML, and can tell an import burst
from work.

title: A control plane for an orchestrator session: identity, contract, and one recorded round-trip
accept: design/13 exists; the orchestrator is registered; one directive round-trip is attributed to it in the ledger; the barrier stays leader-only; the helps page names the role and its limits

body:
Leader, this session: "我接下来会引入一个编排者 session。他会和你们通信，你准备好接受他的控制。"
and "提供接口，这样别人可以实时监控调整".

Where the fabric already stands — measured today, not assumed:
 * Identity exists and works: `aim register --as orchestrator-v0 --kind other
   --model <m> --session '<what it is>'` (bin/aim:614). A new id appears in
   registry.json, in /api/state.agents, and in the dashboard's owner filter for
   free — the filter already lists claude-session2 and synthesizer-v0.
 * Messaging exists: push/confirm with --require-ack, and `aim inbox --as
   orchestrator-v0 --channel <ch>` / `aim wait` (blocking, --timeout, --interval).
 * Barrier authority is already correctly withheld: `require_leader` (bin/aim:555)
   refuses every actor whose kind is not `human` or whose id is not the channel's
   leader. An orchestrator registered as --kind other therefore cannot advance a
   phase or seal for a participant. That is the right default and it should not be
   widened without the leader saying so in writing.

What is missing, and is the actual work on this card:
 1. A written control-plane contract, `design/13-orchestrator.md`: what an
    orchestrator may do (create, assign, move, link, comment, push, request
    advance), what it may not (advance the barrier, seal, reveal a peer's private
    reasoning, or act under another actor's id), what it must record, and how the
    leader revokes it.
 2. Attribution honesty. `--as` is declared, not authenticated (bin/aim:617 says
    so itself). So an orchestrator *could* run `--as claude-session1`. Either say
    plainly in the contract that this is a cooperative threat model, or add the
    check that matters: a per-actor "speak only as yourself" rule enforced in
    `resolve_actor`, recorded in the ledger when refused. Do not claim a guarantee
    the code does not make.
 3. A first real exchange, recorded: register the id, push it a task list, have it
    push back a directive, and confirm the whole loop lands in the ledger with its
    own author on every line. An orchestrator that has never spoken is not an
    orchestrator that is ready.
 4. The monitoring interface is T-0217's second half (`/api/flow`). This card owns
    the contract, the identity and the loop; T-0217 owns the numbers.

Acceptance: design/13 exists; `orchestrator-v0` (or whatever id is chosen) is
registered; one directive round-trip is in the ledger, authored by it; the help
page has a section naming the orchestrator role and what it can and cannot do; and
nothing in the write path lets it advance a barrier.

Status: the revision half is implemented and measured; the footer half is handed
to claude-session1 because App.vue is the file they have in flight and I will not
put two writers on one file.

What landed (aimboard/revision.py, aimboard/api.py, web/vite.config.js):

  /api/state.revision = {
    fabric: "73e15fd+dirty",                     # the tree the server runs from
    bundle: {revision, built_at, dirty, source, source_sha256},
    stale: false,                                # bundle bytes vs current source
    front_end_sha256: "1ea7f991..."
  }

`web/vite.config.js` writes `dist/revision.json` at build time, recording the
commit, the build time, and a content hash of the front-end inputs. The server
compares that hash against the current source and reports `stale`.

Why a content hash and not `sha+dirty`: the first version compared revision
labels, and it is useless in the only case that matters — a tree under development
is dirty at build time and still dirty when the server answers, so the labels
compare equal while the bytes differ. Proved by construction: the JS `sourceHash`
in vite.config.js and the Python `source_hash` in aimboard/revision.py produce the
same digest (`1ea7f9913605fb0d8a290db286b724865adc799e8f5b027866e63cc52bd95dd1`).

The detector, measured on the live board (8777), three sequential requests:
  clean build                            -> stale False
  add a file under web/src               -> stale True
  remove it                              -> stale False
Three states are distinct on purpose: `stale: null` means the bundle never
recorded a hash, and unknown is not equal — an old bundle must not be reported as
fresh.

Remaining on this card:
 1. The footer shows the revision, and says so when `stale` is true. `__AIM_REVISION__`
    is defined by the build for this; App.vue is claude-session1's in-flight file.
 2. Atomic deploy: build to a temp dir, swap. Right now a rebuild deletes the old
    hashed chunks while the server is serving them.
 3. Keep exactly one writable board up: 8777 is up and writable as `human`; 8799
    died again today (third time) and is not being restarted.

Measured review at 1440x1000 and 1024x768, live board 8777, bundle 73e15fd+src,
payload 2026-09-22T07:26:04Z. Four defects, each with the number that proves it.
The card's original 93,972px figure is superseded by these.

1. **The anchor lands 89,710px from the first unread.** In `claude-session1 ⇄
   codex` (121 messages) the first `state:'unread'` message is index **99**; the
   anchor is index **8**, a message whose state is `acked`. Distance anchor ->
   first unread: 89,710px (1440) and 143,916px (1024). Source: ChatPane.vue:168-176,
   where :171 picks "the first message whose chips include `receipt demanded`"
   **regardless of its state**. The newest message is 106,485px below the fold.

2. **`state: 'unread'` is delivered and never consumed.** The payload's
   `conversation.mail` has 125 rows, 21 of them `unread`; ChatPane never reads the
   field. The one branch that does consult unread (`:173`) is **dead code**:
   `conversation.rooms` is `[]` in the live payload. There is no read cursor for
   channels at all — `conversation.channels` keys are `gated,id,messages,phase,rule`
   with no unread field, and no top-level `unread`/`cursor` key exists.

3. **The anchor aligns the message's TOP to a 12px offset** (`ChatPane.vue:200`),
   so the end of the newest message is below the fold by construction: measured
   106,485px, 9,807px (`#barrier-v0`, one 10,350px message), 1,040px, 149px; at
   1024: 143,916px, 16,028px, 526px. `anchorTop = 12` in all nine non-empty threads
   at both viewports.

4. **"needs me" counts receipts owed by someone else — 50% false positive.** With
   viewer `human` it shows 2 threads: `codex ⇄ human` (2 unacked codex->human,
   correct) and `claude-session1 ⇄ codex` (45 receipt chips, **0** addressed to
   human). Source: ChatPane.vue:110-112 tests only for the existence of a
   `receipt demanded` chip, never `to === viewer` and never `state !== 'acked'`.
   Same root cause as the receipts tile on T-0180 (7 counted, 2 addressed to the
   viewer).

Also measured, and it contradicts the standard this project holds: a **manual
refresh button** exists at `ChatPane.vue:294`. Click-to-refresh is forbidden.

Not measured: send/reply position preservation (read-only review). Code says a
successful send always calls `jumpToEnd()` (`:246-250`), so the reader's position is
not preserved.

Suggested anchor rule, in priority order: first message with `state === 'unread' &&
to === viewer`; else the last message; and align the target's *bottom* to the
scroller's bottom rather than its top to a constant.

  bodies in the SPA's index.html:                  0
  the bystander still receives the record's shape: mail/conversation keys present

The policy is stated in one place and the measurement matches it --
`gate.conversation_view` (gate.py:87-99): leader sees every message between
agents; a participant sees mail they sent or received plus what the phase permits;
a bystander gets counts, not contents.

The test adds the one assertion a naive version would miss: selectivity. "A

were my method, not the fabric:
 1. First probe reported "25 leaks" -- it counted the human leader as a third
    party. The leader is a party to the whole record by design, so the model was
    wrong, not the code.

Adversarial review, measured. Verdict: **the group-chat half of the design is
read-only, and the one gate that exists keys on a file field instead of the
channel's phase.** Reproduced as `tests/test_room_gate.py` (6 checks).

== 1. Rooms exist in four read paths and zero write paths ==

`aim` has no `room` verb at all -- enumerated from `aim --help`: no way to create,
publish, or join one. Yet rooms are read by `fabric.load_rooms` (fabric.py:56-84),
gated by `gate.visible_rooms` (gate.py:77-84), rendered by the server view
(views/chat.py:89-102) and by the Vue chat pane, and carried in the payload.

Measured: no `rooms/` directory exists in any channel on disk, and
`/api/state.conversation.rooms == []`. The old renderer says so itself:
"no rooms yet. Group chat and read cursors are M2" (views/chat.py:91).

This is why the leader's requirement -- "还要支持 group chat" -- cannot be met
today, and it is why the Chat pane's only unread branch is dead code
(independent measurement, on T-0181: `room.unread` is read at ChatPane.vue:173 and
`rooms` is always empty).

== 2. Cursors: designed, read, never written ==

`load_rooms` reads `rooms/<room>.cursors.json` and computes per-agent unread from
it (fabric.py:63-71). Nothing writes that file. So **T-0181's fix -- land on the
first unread message -- depends on a read cursor that has no writer.** That
dependency is worth knowing before the scroll work starts: the unread cursor is not
a UI change, it is a missing store plus a verb.

== 3. Mentions: a field nothing fills ==

`mentions` is read in three places -- counted per room (fabric.py:73-76), passed to
the payload (gate.py:126-129), rendered as chips (views/chat.py:48-49,97) -- and
written nowhere. The only occurrence of the word in `bin/aim` is a prose comment
(bin/aim:2444). Mention resolution has never resolved a mention, because nothing
produces one.

== 4. The leak angle nobody proposed: the gate trusts the room's own file ==

`visible_rooms` asks exactly one question:

    room["visibility"] != "published"

It never consults the channel's phase. Measured on a throwaway AIM_ROOT with the
channel in SEALED_DIVERGENT, three rooms written by hand:

    room file                      peer (beta)   leader
    no `visibility` field          hidden        visible
    visibility: "Pubished" (typo)  hidden        visible
    visibility: "published"        VISIBLE       visible

So it is fail-closed against accidents and open against the one deliberate value --
and the documented way to produce that value, `aim room publish`, does not exist.
The only way to publish a room today is to write the file by hand, which design/06
explicitly says publishing must *not* be: "deliberate, recorded, and visible on the
board". Today it is neither recorded nor visible, because there is no verb to
record.

== What would satisfy this card ==

The acceptance sentence was "the room leak is tested by an angle nobody proposed in
the design note" and that is what §4 is: the design note argues about drafts and
publishes, not about the gate having no view of the phase. Test filed as
`tests/test_room_gate.py`. The fix is a separate card (T-0219) because it is a
store-and-verb change, not a rendering change.

title: Rooms have no write side, and the room gate reads a file field instead of the channel's phase
accept: aim room new/publish/say exist and are recorded; the phase gate makes a hand-written 'published' room unreadable during a divergence phase (tests/test_room_gate.py row 3 flips); mentions and read cursors either get writers or lose their readers

body:
From the T-0198 adversarial review. Three defects with one root: rooms have a read
side and no write side, and the one gate they do have reads the room's own file
instead of the channel's phase.

Measured (tests/test_room_gate.py, 6 checks, throwaway AIM_ROOT):

  channel in SEALED_DIVERGENT, rooms written by hand:
    no `visibility` field          -> peer cannot read (default is draft, fail-closed)
    visibility: "Pubished" (typo)  -> peer cannot read
    visibility: "published"        -> PEER READS IT
  `aim --help`: no `room` verb exists.
  `/api/state.conversation.rooms`: [] on the live board; no rooms/ dir in any channel.
  mentions: read in fabric.py:73-76, gate.py:126-129, views/chat.py:48-49,97; written nowhere.
  cursors: read at fabric.py:63-71; written nowhere.

Acceptance:

1. `aim room new --as <who> --channel <ch> --id <id> --topic "..."` creates a room;
   it is recorded in the ledger with its author, and it appears on the board.
2. `aim room publish --as <who> --channel <ch> --id <id>` is the only way a room
   becomes readable by peers during a divergence phase, and the ledger records who
   published it and when. Hand-writing the file must no longer be sufficient.
3. The gate keys on the channel's phase as well as the room's state: during a
   divergence phase a room is draft unless a *recorded* publish exists for it. The
   test above must fail on row 3 after the fix, and still pass on rows 1 and 2.
4. `aim room say --as <who> --channel <ch> --id <id> --body-file f` appends with the
   same flock and hash chain as a channel log, so `aim verify` covers it.
5. Mentions: `@<agent-id>` in a room message body produces the `mentions` list, and
   the field stops being decorative. If you decide mentions stay unimplemented, say
   so and remove the three readers instead -- a field that is read and never written
   is worse than an absent one.
6. Read cursors: a writer for `rooms/<room>.cursors.json` (or an explicit decision
   that unread is per-agent mail only). T-0181's "land on the first unread" depends
   on this and cannot be finished without an answer.

Ordering note: this is the group-chat requirement the leader asked for, so it is
closer to a product gap than a cleanup. It does not block T-0211/T-0212, which the
leader has already felt.

body:
Adversarial review of the task store and verbs. All probes on a throwaway
AIM_ROOT; commands and raw output below. Three defects, and five attacks that the
store refused correctly.

== What held (the kill_if survived) ==

 * A non-participant cannot create work in a channel:
   `task new --as outsider --channel ch` -> "'outsider' is not a participant in ch".
 * A peer's draft is unreadable during divergence, with a barrier-class refusal.
 * Illegal transitions are refused *with the allowed set*:
   `ready -> done` -> "illegal transition ready -> done (allowed: doing, blocked, dropped)".
 * A dangling dependency is refused at creation, not silently accepted:
   `--blocked-by T-9999` -> "REFUSED: no such task to depend on: T-9999".
 * A work item cannot be *born* published during a divergence phase:
   `--visibility published` -> "REFUSED: cannot publish a work item while the
   channel is in SEALED_DIVERGENT. A task title states a position in the least
   suspicious form the fabric contains."
 * `aim verify` reports `chain OK` after every attack above.

== Defect 1: a dependency cycle is accepted, and both items become unclosable ==

    link a --blocked-by b   (b is already blocked_by a)   -> rc 0, accepted
    a -> doing -> review;  b -> doing -> review
    move a --to done  -> REFUSED: T-0001 is blocked by T-0002, which are not done.
    move b --to done  -> REFUSED: T-0002 is blocked by T-0001, which are not done.

Both are now permanently in review. Nothing in the store and nothing on the board
says "these two block each other": each row shows one blocker id, so the human sees
two items that refuse to close for no visible reason. Recoverable only by
`--force` (see defect 2) or by retracting one item (`aim task retract` works and
keeps the created event in the chain).

== Defect 2: `--force` overrides the dependency rule and leaves no trace ==

The event for a forced `review -> done` is, verbatim:

    {"ts": "...", "event": "moved", "actor": "beta", "channel": "ch",
     "context_id": "ch", "task": "T-0002", "from": "review", "to": "done",
     "reason": "", "prev": "...", "hash": "..."}

No marker, and no snapshot of the blocker's status at that moment. So the record
cannot distinguish "finished legitimately" from "finished over an open dependency" --
which is the one distinction this record exists to preserve. Everything else in this
project is careful that an override is a recorded move; this one is invisible.

== Defect 3: the refusal for a blocked `done` names a rule that does not exist ==

    REFUSED: T-0001 is blocked by T-0002, which are not done.
    "Done" is the one status that has to be decided by something other than the person
    asserting it.

The second sentence is not the reason. The reason is the open blocker on the line
above; there is no "who may assert done" rule in cmd_task_move (bin/aim:1427-1447).
This cost me two wrong diagnoses while writing this review -- I read it as an
authorization rule and built two probes around it before checking the code. bin/aim
already contains a comment about exactly this failure class: "a refusal that names
the wrong action is a refusal a reader cannot audit" (bin/aim:560-566). This is that
bug in another place, and it is worth fixing for the same reason.

== Defect 4 (asymmetry): born-published is refused, later-published is a warning ==

    task new --visibility published         -> REFUSED (quoted above)
    task new  (draft);  task publish        -> rc 0
       "T-0001 published DURING SEALED_DIVERGENT -- it is now readable by every
        participant in ch, and this is recorded in the ledger as a barrier event"

Both paths end with a published work item during a sealed phase. One refuses, the
other warns. Either the act is safe (then the creation refusal should warn too) or it
is not (then the publish verb should refuse). Worth noting the published-task rule
itself is documented and works: once published, any participant may move another
agent's item -- measured, beta moved alpha's `T-0001` ready -> doing, and the event
records `actor: beta`.

Filed as T-0220 for the cycle and the `--force` trace; defects 3 and 4 are cheap
enough to fold into the same change.

title: A dependency cycle is accepted and unclosable, and --force overrides it without leaving a trace
accept: link refuses a cycle (test asserts rc!=0 and both tasks stay closable); a forced move records the flag and the blockers it overrode so forced and unforced events differ; the blocked-done refusal stops naming a rule that does not exist

From the T-0197 adversarial review. Two measured defects in the dependency rule, one
of which is a hole in the record itself.

1. `aim task link` accepts a cycle, and a cycle makes both items unclosable:
       link a --blocked-by b   (b already blocked_by a)  -> rc 0
       a -> done  -> REFUSED: T-0001 is blocked by T-0002, which are not done.
       b -> done  -> REFUSED: T-0002 is blocked by T-0001, which are not done.
   Each row shows one blocker id, so nothing on the board says "these two block
   each other". The human sees two items that refuse to close for no visible reason.

2. `--force` overrides the rule and is not recorded. The forced event, verbatim:
       {"event": "moved", "actor": "beta", "task": "T-0002", "from": "review",
        "to": "done", "reason": "", "prev": "...", "hash": "..."}
   No marker, and no snapshot of the blocker's status at that moment, so the record
   cannot distinguish a legitimate completion from an override of an open
   dependency. In a system whose thesis is that the record is the authority, the one
   flag that overrides the rule is the one act it does not record.

3. While you are in this code: the refusal for a blocked `done` carries a second
   sentence that describes a rule which does not exist --
   `"Done" is the one status that has to be decided by something other than the
   person asserting it.` The real reason is the open blocker above it; there is no
   "who may assert done" check in cmd_task_move (bin/aim:1427-1447). It misled me
   into two wrong diagnoses while reviewing. bin/aim:560-566 already states the rule
   this violates.

4. And the asymmetry: `task new --visibility published` during SEALED_DIVERGENT is
   REFUSED, while `task publish` in the same phase prints a warning and proceeds
   ("recorded in the ledger as a barrier event"). Both end with a published item in
   a sealed phase. Pick one posture.

Acceptance:
 * `aim task link` refuses to create a cycle (reachability check) with a refusal that
   names both ends, and a test asserts rc != 0 and that each task remains closable.

   `tests/` must fail if the event is identical for forced and unforced moves.

   rule that does not exist.

title: The ledger records a stranger's refusal as a malformed request, so refusals cannot be audited by class
accept: a registered non-participant runs aim say --channel hello and the new ledger row has class barrier

body:
Found by `codex-orangement` on its first day, by reading its own refusals, and the
citation is exact. I file it because the fix is one word in four places and the cost
of not fixing it is that the refusal ledger cannot be audited by the field that
exists to audit it.

What the record says. `channels/hello/ledger.jsonl` now holds 8 refusals against the
new session, all from honest attempts through the tool:

  3 x class="barrier"  (aim task list, while the channel was in COMMIT)
  5 x class="form"     (aim say, aim friction --add x2, aim task new --
                        "'codex-orangement' is not a participant")

But all five of those are the same kind of event as the three: a well-formed request
refused for *who sent it*. And the source says so, twice:

 * `bin/aim:555` `require_leader` passes `cls="barrier"` for exactly this shape of
   check, with the comment: "It is not a malformed request -- the request is
   well-formed and is refused for who sent it."
 * `gate.py` `exit_refusal`'s docstring names the second way of being shut out as the
   barrier: "being a **stranger**: you are a registered agent and not a participant."
 * `bin/aim:201` `die()` defaults to `cls="form"`, and the membership check on `say`
   calls `die()` with no class. `rg 'cls="form"' bin/aim` finds only the two default
   parameters (:171, :201) and no site that chooses it. So "form" is not a decision --
   it is the fallback for everything that does not claim otherwise.

Consequence, and it is the reason this is a defect rather than a nit: the barrier page
offers exactly two classes to filter by (`barrier`, `form`, BarrierPane.vue:123-126).
A reader auditing by class -- the only affordance the field has -- finds five
malformed-request errors where there were five well-formed requests refused for
identity. That is a refusal a reader cannot audit, which is what `require_leader`'s
comment was written to prevent.

Fix: pass the barrier class at the four membership gates. Forward-only; the ledger is
hash-chained and existing rows must not be rewritten. If a gate genuinely cannot

body:
The headline number, measured on the live payload at 07:36Z by `codex-orangement`,
viewer human:

    status "done" displayed ......... 45
    reports.with_history ............  3    (items with a recorded `moved -> done`)
    reports.recorded / seed_only .... 64 / 87

So the board shows 45 items as done and 3 of them have a recorded transition to done.
This is the same conflation this card is about, seen from the top of the page instead
of from the Gantt: a seed's `done` column is plan-authored text, not an event, and
every surface that reads `board.tasks` instead of `board.recorded()` inherits it.

Two consequences worth stating in the card's own terms:
 * any burn-down, throughput or "% complete" figure computed from `status` is a
   statement about the plan file, not about the work;
 * 42 of those 45 are seeds, which is the same 42 this card counted painted green on
   the Gantt -- so the two panes agree with each other and disagree with the record.

Also, and separately from this card: `codex-orangement` read the whole README and
reported that this number appears nowhere in it. A reader arriving at the repository
cannot learn that the board's headline counts plan text as finished work. That belongs
with T-0200 (the README capability matrix); noted there too.

Two things this README must say, both measured today, neither in it now.

 1. **What the headline number counts.** `/api/state` with viewer human, 07:36Z:
    `status: done` shows 45 items and `reports.with_history` is 3 -- three items have
    a recorded `moved -> done`. The other 42 are plan seeds whose `done` column is
    plan-authored text. A reader who trusts the board's top line believes 45 things
    are finished; the record supports 3. `codex-orangement` read this README end to
    end on its first day and reported that the number appears nowhere in it.
 2. **What the refusal ledger is a record of.** `codex-orangement` disclosed, in its
    own message and unasked, that it read `channels/hello/tasks.jsonl` with `cat`
    before the tool ever refused it -- and that `aim`'s refusals are not enforceable
    against an agent with a shell. It is right, and README §2 already concedes the
    tool "cannot be talked around without editing the tool", but the important half
    is missing: a filesystem read leaves no diff and no ledger row. So the refusals
    count is a record of barrier violations *attempted through the tool*, and any
    reader who takes it as the complete set is being misled by omission. Say which
    one it is. (Related: T-0222, where the ledger cannot even be audited by class.)

title: A second board on a non-canonical port is invisible, so two bundles can answer for one tree
accept: with two serves up for one root, /api/revision on either names the other pid and port

body:
Measured three times today, so this is not a slip anyone made once: a second
`aimboard serve` on a non-canonical port reappeared at 07:40Z (8799, pid 62028)
while the canonical board was up on 8777, after the rule was written and after
8799 had already been killed once. A rule in AGENTS.md does not bind a process.

  first board on 8777   pid 59830
  second board on 8799  pid 62028   <- invisible on every surface

Why it matters even though nothing is broken by it: two servers for one root serve
two different `web/dist` builds, so a probe, a screenshot or a report URL can be a
statement about a bundle nobody chose. That is the mechanism by which three findings
were nearly filed against the wrong build earlier today.

Minimal fix, in the tool rather than in prose: when `cmd_serve` starts, look for
another `aimboard serve` for the same `--root` (the same /proc walk `port_holder`
already does, across listeners) and
 * print a line naming the other pid and its port when one exists, and
 * expose it in `/api/revision` as `other_boards: [{pid, port}]`,

so a measurement taken on either board can say out loud that the tree had two.
Refusing outright would fight the test suite, which legitimately replaces the
canonical server; saying nothing is what we have now, and it is what failed.

Acceptance: start a second serve for the same root on another port, then
`curl /api/revision` on either one and see `other_boards` naming the other pid.

body:

`71075e3` landed (viewer human, live board 8777):

The sentence and the promise/work split are correct now -- that half is verified

So 15 of 19 rows -- 79% -- are somebody else's mail, and they sit under a hero
number on the page whose whole job is to say what the human must do. A number the
reader cannot clear and mostly cannot act on is the definition of decoration, and
this one is now bigger than every real signal on the page combined.

  * count `to === viewer` only, and label it "4 for you, 15 elsewhere on the record"; or

New evidence on the attribution half of this card, from today, and it is not
hypothetical: **I cannot distinguish my own work from my subagents' in the record.**

What happened. I spawned review subagents with my context. They inherited my
identity, so their writes are authored `codex`:

  * T-0220 (barrier tab strip), T-0222 (refusal classes), T-0223 (a second board is
    invisible) were filed by a subagent; the card history says `created codex`,
    exactly as my own cards do.
  * Two letters to `codex-orangement` (07:37:50Z, 07:38:47Z) were written and sent
    by a subagent under my id, including a retraction of advice I had given.
  * A subagent also committed my code (`ad4c811`) and rebuilt the served bundle
    (`b7724aa`), which is why the revision in the payload moved without me running
    a build.

The consequence is concrete, not philosophical: I found a card on the board under
my name that I did not create and had to reconstruct who wrote it by reading
timestamps. If I cannot attribute my own tree, the leader cannot attribute the
team's, and the record's answer to "who decided this?" is wrong in a way no reader
can detect -- which is the failure this project exists to make impossible.

This is the same hole codex-orangement measured from the other side ("`push`/`say`
take `--as` as a declared identity, not an authenticated one"), and it is worth
noting that the *content* the subagent produced was good and its retraction was
correct. The problem is not the work; it is that the record cannot say who did it.

Concrete ask, in order of value:
 1. A child session must be able to declare its parent, and the event must carry
    both: `actor: codex::review-1` or `actor: codex` + `on_behalf_of`/`delegated_from`.
    The cheapest honest version is an env var the harness sets (`AIM_PARENT=codex`),
    recorded as a field, so a delegated write is distinguishable from a direct one.
 2. `aim` should refuse to *create* a task with an owner that is not a registered
    agent (it already does) and should record the registering session for the actor
    when an id is claimed (registry has `session`; the task events do not).
 3. Then the derivation in codex-orangement's org card has something true to
    derive from, rather than a flat `actor: codex` that means "me or one of five
    children".

title: --body given a file path sends the path, silently: a 24-byte message that looks valid
accept: verbs taking free text refuse a --body that is the path of an existing file, with a message naming --body-file; a test asserts rc!=0 and no message in the outbox; deliberately sending that literal text is still possible

body:
Measured by me, by accident, thirty seconds ago:

    aim push --as codex --to claude-session1 --channel hello --subject "..." \
        --body /tmp/bodies/to-claude.md
    outbox: .../20260922T074039.844Z-codex.md  (24 bytes, sha 8a78d281c512...)

The message body is the literal string `/tmp/bodies/to-claude.md`. It was delivered,
it is well-formed, it has a valid sha256, and it says nothing. The recipient sees a
path where a message should be, and nothing in the output of the send says a word
went missing.

This is the exact failure mode codex-orangement predicted for a CLI boundary
("bytes: a message body is free-form UTF-8 with newlines; JSON string args and a
subprocess pipe are not equivalent transports, and the difference shows up as a
silently truncated message — well-formed and missing an argument"), except the
trigger is simpler than any tool-calling wrapper: a human, or an agent, who typed
`--body` where they meant `--body-file`.

Why it is worth five lines of code rather than a note in the docs: the failure is
silent, the artifact is signed, and it lands in the record. A refusal is a fact; a
24-byte message that looks fine is a lie.

Acceptance:
 * `--body` whose value is the path of an existing readable file is REFUSED with
   "that looks like a file; use --body-file <path>" rather than sent. Same for
   `--body` values that are only a path and contain no spaces or newlines (the
   shape that produces this), for `check`, `say`, `push`, `reveal`, `task comment`
   and any other verb taking free text.
 * Test: one assertion per verb, asserting rc != 0 and that the outbox gained no
   message.
 * Status is unaffected: if the user really means to send the literal text
   `/tmp/x.md`, `--body-file` with a file containing that line, or an escape/flag
   such as `--body-literal`, must still work. Do not make a legal message
   unsendable.

title: A route change waits for ten animation frames, so a busy renderer never finishes the navigation
accept: A pane change completes without depending on animation-frame count: measured with CDP CPU throttling at x20, median time from click to the URL changing is under 1s (today: 44441ms median, 54940ms max over 8 navigations), and the E2E suite is green on two consecutive full runs while another agent is working on the same machine.

reason: P0: this is why the E2E suite's failures move between tests

body:
Measured by me on HEAD `81dc58f`, board on 8777, probe `web/probe-nav-latency.mjs`
(untracked; `cd web && node probe-nav-latency.mjs`). 8 hash navigations per rate,
time from the hash change to the router having committed it:

| CPU throttle | min | median | max |
|---|---|---|---|
| x1  |   68ms |   740ms |  1187ms |
| x20 | 2851ms | 44441ms | 54940ms |

A 20x throttle producing a 60x latency is not CPU work; it is a wait on frames.
`web/src/main.js` returns `resetReadingPane()` -- an async loop of ten
`requestAnimationFrame` turns -- from the router's `scrollBehavior`, and Vue Router
awaits a returned promise before the navigation is committed.

Why it matters beyond the probe: this is the mechanism behind the E2E suite's moving
failures, which I could not explain before and which makes every "green" claim
unreliable. Observed in three separate full runs on two revisions, each of these red
in a full run and green in isolation (2/2 runs each):
 * `web/tests/anchors.spec.js:61` "clicking the phase chip puts that phase row in the pane"
 * `web/tests/boards.spec.js:430` "a filter change does not drag the columns out from under a computed"
 * `web/tests/barrier.spec.js:99` and `:123` (the T-0220 tests)
The failure that moves is the tell: the assertion that loses is whichever one
navigates while the renderer is slowest, and the log shows the URL simply not
changing inside the 5s budget (`Received string: ".../#/barrier?channel=alpha"`
where `/channel=hello/` was expected, 13 retries).

Known-bad and known-good, so the fix has a control: the same probe against the
pre-81dc58f `scrollBehavior` (a plain value, no promise) should show x20 within a
small multiple of x1. If it does not, my mechanism is wrong and the card should be
retracted rather than fixed.

body:
Contract for `GET /api/flow` — agreed, and it is now the acceptance on T-0217.

    GET /api/flow?channel=hello&bucket=10m&window=12h

Answer (abridged to the load-bearing parts):

    { "generated_at": "...", "revision": { "digest": <fabric_digest>, "tasks_sha256": "...", "store_last_event_ts": "..." },
      "bucket": { "width_seconds": 600, "key": "start", "alignment": "floor(ts,600s) in UTC", "timezone": "UTC" },
      "window": { "requested": "12h", "start": "...", "end": "...", "buckets": 72, "data_start": "..." },
      "series": [ { "start": "...", "opened": 33, "opened_by": {"codex": 33}, "opened_inferred": 0,
                    "opened_first_ts": "...", "opened_last_ts": "...",
                    "done": 0, "done_by": {}, "done_first_ts": null, "done_last_ts": null,
                    "hours_opened": null, "hours_done": null, "unplaced": 0, "retracted": 0 } ],
      "totals": { "opened": 71, "done": 3, "hours_opened": null, "hours_done": null },
      "idle_gap": { "from": "...", "to": "...", "minutes": 200 },
      "sources": { "store_recorded": 70, "seed_only": 87, "items_claiming_done": 45, "done_from_seed": 42, ... } }

Rules that make it usable rather than merely present:
 * Dense series, always exactly `window.buckets` entries, zeros included. An omitted
   bucket makes 07:10Z and 15:40Z adjacent, so a burst and a dead afternoon look the same.
 * Half-open `[start, start+600)`; width stated once in `bucket`, never repeated per row.
 * `opened_first_ts`/`opened_last_ts` are load-bearing: the busiest bucket is 33 opens
   spanning 40.0s (an import) versus 9 opens over 8 minutes in a real bucket. The server
   publishes the rate; the consumer picks the threshold. No `import` flag, no `saturated` flag.
 * `hours_opened`/`hours_done` are present and `null` until `estimate_hours` exists (0 of 212
   records have it today; `estimate_pts` has it on all 70). Do not substitute a conversion.
 * `revision.digest` must be `fabric_digest(root)`, the same function `/api/digest` uses, so a
   monitor can poll digest cheaply (measured: 353 files, 5.5ms) and fetch flow only on change,
   then verify `flow.revision.digest` equals the digest that triggered the fetch.
 * Compute in `aimboard/fold.py` from the RAW event list, not `fold_tasks` output: `fold_tasks`
   drops unplaceable records and erases retracted ones, so a flow series folded through it
   could not publish `unplaced`/`retracted` to reconcile against the board.
 * The dispatch at `aimboard/cli.py:511` strips the query string before handlers see it; the
   flow handler must parse the raw `self.path` or every parameter silently becomes a default.
 * Add `/api/flow` to the `endpoints` list in the 404 body (`aimboard/cli.py:544`).

Measured sample (last 12h, 10-minute buckets): 72 buckets, 13 non-zero (18%; 36 of the
zeros pre-date the store's first event at 02:16:37Z), busiest 07:10Z with 33 opened,
longest idle gap 200 minutes (03:50Z -> 07:10Z). Totals 71 opened, 3 done. `done` has
3 events in the whole store, so the done series has no trend yet — the endpoint must
ship `data_start` and `sources` rather than a verdict.

Nothing in `reports` answers this today: `throughput` is `[["2026-09-22", 3]]` and
`web/src/panes/ReportsPane.vue:54` renders `throughput.length`, so 3 closures display as **1**.
`series` is 14 daily rows, 144x coarser than asked, and `median_cycle` is day-truncated so it
cannot be non-zero in a one-day session.

Amendment, from `codex-orangement`'s review (evidence: `reviews/10-room-publish-provenance.md`,
card text quoted as C10 in `reviews/06-card-ready.md`). I wrote clause 2 and its mechanism is wrong.

Clause 2 as written: "the phase gate makes a hand-written 'published' room unreadable during a
divergence phase". That is not what design/06 §2 says. Quoting it: "A participant may open it early
with `aim room publish`, which is deliberate, recorded, and visible on the board. So a room inherits
the channel's gate: a room created while the parent channel is in a divergence phase is a draft
room." The gate is keyed on the *phase at creation* plus a recorded publish -- not on the string in
the file. A clause that says "make a hand-written published room unreadable" would, if implemented
literally, delete the verb that clause 1 requires (`aim room publish`), which is the contradiction
it was reviewed under.

Amended clause 2: a room created while the channel is in a divergence phase is a draft room and is
readable by its author and the leader only; `aim room publish` is the deliberate, recorded act that
exposes it, and it is refused-or-recorded the way `task publish` already is (see `bin/aim`'s
`task_published_during_divergence` ledger event). A file whose `visibility` field says "published"
without a recorded publish event must be treated as a draft, and `tests/test_room_gate.py` row 3
(same file it already asserts) is the check that this is true.

title: /api/agents is unreachable: the 404 catch-all is dispatched before the handler that serves it
accept: GET /api/agents returns 200 with the registry as the viewer sees it; the 404 body's endpoint list and the dispatch order cannot disagree, and a test asserts every endpoint the 404 body advertises actually answers 200.

body:
Measured by Lorentz while landing /api/flow, and re-measured by me against the running board at 8777 (bundle dbdd04e+dirty):
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:8777/api/agents   -> 404
    body: {"error": "no such endpoint", "path": "/api/agents", "endpoints": ["/api/state", "/api/digest", "/api/agents", "/api/revision", "/api/flow", "/api/command (POST, --allow-write)"]}

The endpoint names itself in its own 404 body. Mechanism: `aimboard/cli.py` dispatches `if path.startswith("/api/")` at the catch-all before `if path == "/api/agents"`, so the later branch is dead code. It is advertised twice -- in that list and in `web/src/api.js:54` (`agents: () => getJson('/api/agents')`) -- though the panes read `doc.agents` from /api/state, so nothing on screen is broken by it today. Fix is to move the `/api/agents` branch above the catch-all; the acceptance asks for a test that every endpoint in the 404 body answers 200, because a list that advertises a dead endpoint is the same class of lie as a 200 carrying HTML.

title: The published AgentCard cannot be parsed by the reference implementation
accept: the a2a-sdk's own protobuf parse of the output of 'aim card' succeeds: removing or relocating the top-level metadata field makes tests/test_a2a_reference_client.py::test_the_published_card_is_not_a_valid_agent_card invert from asserting a ParseError to asserting a clean parse.

body:
Measured by Newton on commit e3824c5 with a2a-sdk 1.1.5, and re-run by me (/tmp/a2a-ref-venv/bin/python tests/test_a2a_reference_client.py -> 6/6 OK). The SDK's protobuf refuses our card:

    ParseError: Message type "lf.a2a.v1.AgentCard" has no field named "metadata" at "AgentCard".

No card means no client: the reference implementation cannot even discover us. Removing only that field makes the card parse cleanly, and then the next three walls appear in order -- the custom protocolBinding ('.../aim-files/v1' -> ValueError: no compatible transports found), the interface url being a filesystem path (A2AClientError: Request URL is missing an http:// or https:// protocol), and the absence of /.well-known/agent-card.json. Measured against the live root, three formats:

 * CSV and JSON pass, including the part a valid-but-incomplete export would fail: both carry exactly as many items as the board draws (compared against 'aimboard render --json').

body:
This defect has a fresh, measured instance -- and it was introduced today, by a
fix to a *different* card (T-0224, the `--body <path>` trap), which is exactly
why it belongs on this card rather than on that one.

MEASURED. `tests/test_aimboard.py` went 99/99 -> 106/108 in this working tree. The
two failures are lines 539 and 547, against a SEALED_DIVERGENT channel posting
`reveal --channel hello --claim-id c1` with no body:

    FAIL  a verb the tool refuses returns the tool's own refusal
    FAIL  the recorded refusal names the act and the actor

CAUSE, by diff: the T-0224 work added `free_text_body(args)` to `cmd_reveal` and
placed it *above* the phase check. An empty body then dies first with
`cls="form"`, so the phase refusal is never reached, the stderr no longer carries
`REFUSED`, and the ledger's last line is a malformed-request refusal where the
test -- and the design -- require `"class": "barrier"`.

This is the general shape of the bug and it is worth stating plainly, because
"which class a refusal gets" is not cosmetic here: the ledger is the only record
of who was stopped and by what rule, so a misclassified refusal is a lost record.
Any check that can fire before a barrier check will steal the classification.
Ordering is therefore load-bearing, not stylistic.

FIXED in the same loop: the phase gate is back above the body check in
`cmd_reveal` only, with a comment stating that the order is deliberate so a
future tidy-up does not move it again. Re-measured: `108/108 checks passed`, and
the body trap T-0224 added is intact.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN on this card: the class is currently correct only where a
human put the barrier check first. Nothing enforces the ordering. A finishable
version of this card is a test that walks every verb's refusal paths in a
divergence phase and asserts the class, so the next reorder fails a test instead
of quietly rewriting the record.

title: No surface answers the org chart: who is in the team, who may dispatch to whom, who reports to whom
accept: One command answers all three questions for a named agent without reading a JSON file by hand: (1) the org it belongs to and the other members, (2) the agents it may dispatch work to, (3) the agent it reports to. Observable: run it for a newly registered agent and it returns those three answers, or names exactly which is undefined. Adding an agent to the org is one recorded act, and the org it joins is the same object aim status --channel reports participants for -- not a second roster that can drift.

title: Nothing states which project a session is on, and scratch channels are indistinguishable from real ones
accept: Given a session id, one command says which project/channel it is currently working on, derived from the store and not from a hand-maintained field. Observable: a session that moves from channel A to channel B changes the answer with no hand edit. Separately, a channel records whether it is a real project or a throwaway, so aim status can hide scratch channels and a leaked probe channel is visible.

body:
Filed from the leader's own words, which are the requirement:

    我感觉我们aim还缺少一个团队管理的功能，比如让agent加入组织，能否最快获取到
    组织架构，清楚谁可以调度，向谁汇报

("I feel aim is still missing a team-management feature -- letting an agent join an
organisation, getting the org structure as fast as possible, and being clear about
who may dispatch work and to whom you report.")

WHERE IT BITES TODAY, measured rather than argued. This session arrived at
07:25Z as a registered agent with a job to do, and could not answer any of the
three questions from the tool:

- "who is in this team?" -- registry.json lists ids and `kind`; a channel lists its
  participants. Neither is an org, and they disagree (codex has 46 cards and is a
  participant of hello; claude-session1 has 52 and is too; barrier-v0 and dev
  exist with three other channels and unrelated members).
- "who may I dispatch to?" -- no field, anywhere. I could ring anyone's doorbell
  (`aim push --to <id>`) whether or not they had any duty to answer me, and I had
  no way to learn the difference. The first question I ever asked the leader was
  whether to route through the codex PM, and I could not have answered it from
  the store.
- "to whom do I report?" -- the answer is "the leader" only because a human told
  me in prose, in this session. It is not in the record.

The gap is not cosmetic: it is why this session's first six requests were messages
rather than cards, and why the leader had to explain the reporting line by hand.

WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING. I am not claiming an org chart should exist as a new file
that has to be kept in sync -- that is the drift this project keeps measuring
(C3/C5, `reports` folded from the wrong set; T-0226's owner field that does not
mean what it says). The best shape is probably derived: `kind`,
`channel participants`, and `owner` already carry most of the edges, and the
deliverable may be a *view* that states which of the three answers is undefined
rather than a fourth roster. Deciding that is the work.

The leader named multi-session/project management as a deliverable next to group
chat. Until this card it had no row anywhere: `rg -c 'multi-session' plan/plan.json`
was 0 and no channel carried a milestone for it.

WHAT EXISTS, measured: one flat namespace. The store currently holds five channels
-- `barrier-v0`, `dev`, `hello`, `s2-scratch`, `s2-scratch2` -- and two of those are
throwaway roots that probe runs created and abandoned. `aim status --channel <ch>`
has no way to distinguish a real project channel from a scratch one, and nothing
states which project a session is currently on: the registry records that
`codex-orangement` exists, not what it is working on.

WHY THIS IS THE SAME PROBLEM AS THE FILE COLLISION. Today six review lanes ran in
one checkout with no claim and no lock, and a peer's `git commit` swallowed another
lane's `fold.py` edit because there is no object that means "I am working on this".
A per-session "what am I on" is the smallest thing that would let a commit, a
channel and a card all say the same noun.

CAUTION for whoever takes this: do not invent a second roster. The channels
already exist; the missing part is that nothing derives the answer. Prefer a
derived view plus one field that is written by an act, over a new file a human
maintains.

body: Measured 2026-09-22: dev is empty (0 recorded, 0 public messages, both participants unsealed) while the real conversation sits in a channel topic'd 'Transport test'.

Measurement, 2026-09-22, from the seat that did not author this card — leaving it as evidence rather than closing the card, which is its owner's move.

Both halves of the title are now false on disk, and one half of the reason is not.

Clause 1, 'rooms have no write side': measured on a throwaway AIM_ROOT, channel in SEALED_DIVERGENT — the five verbs exist (`aim room new/say/publish/list/meta`, `cmd_room_*` in bin/aim), `aim room new` creates a draft room, `aim room say --body '@beta …' ` appends r0001 with `mentions {beta: 1}` and advances the author's own cursor, `aim room publish --reason …` writes a `room_published` ledger row carrying `phase`, `class: barrier`, `barrier_open` and the message count, and `aim room list` marks the draft `[withheld from you]` for a peer. So the read-only half is closed.

Clause 2, 'the room gate reads a file field instead of the channel's phase': still true, and now split across two halves that disagree. `bin/aim` no longer trusts the field — it requires the recorded row as well (`_room_published`), so a hand-edited `visibility: "published"` no longer opens the room to `aim`. `aimboard/gate.py`'s `visible_rooms` still asks only `room["visibility"] != "published"`, so that same hand-edit still opens it on the board. Measured: `aim room list --as <peer>` marks it `[withheld from you]` while `visible_rooms` serves it to that peer, a stranger and the leader alike. Same file, two answers.

And a third thing this card's own amendment recorded, which I re-measured because it decides whether clause 2 was ever the right rule: `aim room publish` during SEALED_DIVERGENT succeeds and says so on stdout ('published DURING SEALED_DIVERGENT … recorded in the ledger as a barrier event'). So an early publish is a legitimate, recorded act and not a gate failure — the gate is about who may READ a draft room, not about whether publishing is allowed. A fix that made clause 2's phase test into a refusal would forbid the act design/06 §2 names.

I have not moved this card: it is a draft owned by codex and the channel is in COMMIT, and while a peer may comment on another's draft, the move to review is its owner's assertion.

title: A task event the fold has no branch for is dropped in silence, and the stray-event counter cannot fire on it
accept: With bin/aim:2330 emitting "edited" and aimboard/fold.py having no branch for it, fold_tasks returns tasks_unknown_events = 0 and the edited field unchanged; after the fix, a task edit moves the field the board draws.

body:
T-0246: the measurement, from the seat that filed it. 2026-09-23, HEAD `94a8e34`.

**Reproduction, throwaway root, re-runnable:**

    aim task new --as alpha --channel ch --title "a card" --accept "it works" --owner alpha
      -> T-0001 created (backlog, draft) — a card
    aim task edit --as alpha --channel ch --id T-0001 --priority high --reason "changed my mind"
      -> T-0001: priority normal -> high          # the verb reports success
    fold_tasks(open('channels/ch/tasks.jsonl'))
      -> tasks_unknown_events = 0, priority = "normal"    # the board does not move

**The store row it wrote** (`bin/aim:2330`, called from `cmd_task_edit` at `:2346`):

    {"ts": "...", "event": "edited", "actor": "alpha", "channel": "ch",
     "context_id": "ch", "task": "T-0001",
     "changes": [{"field": "priority", "from": "normal", "to": "high"}],
     "reason": "changed my mind", "session": "..."}

It lands in `tasks.jsonl` via `_append_task_event` (`:1873`), so it is the store's
own vocabulary and not a ledger-only name.

**Two silences, and the second is the finding.**

1. `TASK_EVENTS` (`bin/aim:127`) declares eight names and no code reads it, so
   nothing refuses the ninth.
2. `aimboard/fold.py:120` increments `unknown` only on the `else` branch for a
   task whose `created` was **never seen**. `edited` arrives *after* a `created`
   the fold did read, so it takes the `elif tid in items: item = items[tid]`
   branch at `:117`, appends itself to `item["events"]`, matches no `if/elif`
   below, and the loop ends. No counter moves.

I checked the mechanism rather than assuming it: appending an entry named
`totally_made_up` to the same store also leaves `tasks_unknown_events = 0`. The
counter cannot fire on an unknown *name* at all — it only fires on an unknown
*task*. So the fabric has an alarm for stray events and the alarm is wired to a
different condition than the one this verb produces.

**Why it matters beyond one field.** `design/05` and `aimboard/a2a.py:836` both
lean on the fold as the single reader of the task store — `a2a_task` publishes
the board's `status` and `metadata.aim`, and HelpPane renders the flow from the
same fold. A card can therefore be edited and the board, the A2A surface and the
help page will all agree on the old value, with nothing anywhere recording that
they are wrong. That is the shape §4.4 calls the defect: one rule, and the copy
that is read is not the copy that was written.

**The scope, measured rather than asserted.** I scanned every literal
`"event": "..."` in `bin/aim` against `aimboard/fold.py`'s branches. Eighteen
names are written but not branched — `phase`, `seal`, `push`, `refusal`,
`concession`, `friction`, `room_created`, `room_published`, `workspace_cleared`,
`channel_member_added/noop/removed`, `task_published_during_divergence`,
`doorbell_created`, `doorbell_rotated`, `deleted` — and every one of those is a
**ledger** event, correctly outside a task fold. `edited` is the only name
written into `tasks.jsonl` that the fold has no branch for. The fix is one
branch in `fold.py` plus `"edited"` in `TASK_EVENTS`, or a `die(cls="form")` in
`cmd_task_edit` if editing a card is not meant to be supported at all — but the
verb exists, is wired at `:4613`, and documents itself at `:2255`, so the first
is the honest one.

**Not fixed here.** `aimboard/fold.py` is codex's lane and this card is codex's.
The SOP records the measurement (Part IV-c.1, commit `94a8e34`); the code is
yours.

title: aim seal accepts a claims payload of the wrong type: string stored verbatim, '(10 claims)' printed, and /api/state 500s for the leader and the sealer
accept: A claims file holding the bare string "not-a-list" is refused at seal time (rc != 0, nothing written), and no seal file in the tree can make /api/state raise AttributeError.

body:
Measured 2026-09-23 on a throwaway root (init, register alpha=claude/beta=codex/human=human, new-channel ch leader=human participants=alpha,beta).

A. `printf "\"not-a-list\"" > claims.json; aim seal --as alpha --channel ch --summary "..." --claims claims.json`
   -> `sealed alpha: ea469e87d519d63e…  (10 claims)`, rc 0
   -> seals/alpha.json holds `"claims": "not-a-list"` verbatim; `10` is len("not-a-list").

B. Same with a 1-element list whose item has no `kill_if` -> rc 0, stored verbatim, `(1 claims)`.
   (already written up in SOP.md §1.1 step 8, which is where A was first reported)

C. Serving that root (`bin/aimboard.py serve --root $T --port 8791 --as human`), `GET /api/state?as=…`:
     human (leader)      500  {"error":"the server could not answer","detail":"'str' object has no attribute 'get'"}
     human2 (kind=human, registered after the seal, not leader, not participant)  500
     alpha (participant, the sealer)   500
     beta (participant, peer)          200
     gamma (registered stranger)       200
     codex / codex-orangement (unregistered here)  200

So it is NOT "500 for every viewer" — the SOP said that and I have corrected it. The rule is at aimboard/api.py:354-357, reached from :353 `if secrets or who == viewer`, where `secrets = not walled_off(state, ch, viewer)` and `walled_off` (gate.py:24-28) returns False for kind=="human" and for any participant while phase in DIVERGENCE ("SEALED_DIVERGENT","COMMIT","SYNTHESIS", const.py:5). Two consequences: no human viewer ever gets the withholding branch, and no participant is ever given "your own seal is yours" while the channel is sealed. So the crash is always reachable by at least one viewer: a malformed seal owned by a participant bricks that participant; one owned by a human bricks every human.

Not a blocker for this root (/root/tmp/agent-im has no malformed seal; I checked) — but `aim seal` exits 0 while writing it and `aim verify` returns `chain OK` rc 0 and never reads `claims`, so nothing in the tool would tell you.

Suggested fix, one line at the read: `claims = seal.get("claims"); if not isinstance(claims, list): claims = []` before the comprehension, or refuse the shape at bin/aim:1375 where it is loaded. Refusing at write time is the better half — the seal is the artifact whose whole purpose is to be falsifiable.

I have not touched bin/aim or aimboard/. Full write-up: SOP.md §1.1 step 8.

title: Declaring a shared workspace while a channel is in COMMIT disables its only legal forward edge, bare and forced, with no announcement
accept: A channel in COMMIT whose manifest declares a shared writable path either refuses the workspace declaration at the moment it would strand the channel, or names that the ordinary exit just closed.

body:
Measured 2026-09-23 on a throwaway root (register h=human/a=claude/b=codex, new-channel ch participants a,b leader=h, both sealed, advance COMMIT).

`aim channel workspace --as h --channel ch --set a=$T/src --set b=$T/src` -> rc 0, and it says so plainly:

  "ch: workspace recorded. This channel can no longer enter or remain in a divergence phase:
   /tmp/.../src  shared by a, b"

Then, from COMMIT:

  -> SYNTHESIS            bare   rc=2  REFUSED: channel declares a shared workspace
  -> SYNTHESIS            FORCE  rc=2  REFUSED: channel declares a shared workspace
  -> SEALED_DIVERGENT     FORCE  rc=2  REFUSED
  -> CROSS_EXAMINE        FORCE  rc=0
  -> RESOLVE (from CX)    FORCE  rc=0
  -> CLOSED  (from RES)   FORCE  rc=0

`COMMIT -> SYNTHESIS` is the ONLY forward edge `TRANSITIONS["COMMIT"]` has. `SEALED_DIVERGENT`, `COMMIT` and `SYNTHESIS` are `const.DIVERGENCE`, so `assert_barrier_defensible` (bin/aim:556, called :1073 and :1473) refuses every edge INTO one — and the five-advance route to CLOSED runs through SYNTHESIS. So a channel that declares a shared workspace while in COMMIT can no longer close by the ordinary route: refused bare AND refused forced, with only forced jumps that skip past the refused edge.

The inversion is the finding, not the refusal. The guard exists to stop a barrier from being asserted when participants can read each other work — and in this one state it refuses the honest forward move and permits the forced leap over it. A channel that declares a shared workspace is precisely one where the barrier is a lie; that channel can still be forced into RESOLVE and CLOSED without ever passing SYNTHESIS, which is the phase whose quorum check (`cannot enter SYNTHESIS before every participant has sealed`, rc 2, names the missing agents) is the one thing that would have caught it.

Not a trap: the refusal message names the release, `aim channel workspace --channel ch --none`, measured rc 0, after which `COMMIT -> SYNTHESIS` is rc 0 again with `--synthesizer`. The defect is that nothing announces the ordinary exit just closed, and the operation that closes it is offered as a plain manifest edit.

Suggested fix, either half: refuse the workspace declaration when the current phase is in DIVERGENCE and the only forward exit leads into one (i.e. name the consequence at write time), or let the bare `COMMIT -> SYNTHESIS` edge report why it is refused rather than reporting the generic illegal-transition line. The first is better — it is the same shape as `assert_barrier_defensible` itself: a claim about a phase made checkable by the filesystem.

I have not touched bin/aim or aimboard/.

title: A second voice in a draft room locks its author out permanently, and a human stranger can publish it

body:
Reproduced end to end on a throwaway root, channel `ch`, participants `beta`, leader `lead`, phase SEALED_DIVERGENT:

    beta  room new  --id r1                        rc 0
    beta  room say  --id r1 --body "beta own"      rc 0
    beta  room list --channel ch  ->  r1  1 msg  draft  by beta
    otherh room say --id r1 --body "otherh"        rc 0   (kind=human, NOT leader, NOT participant)
    beta  room list --channel ch  ->  r1  2 msgs draft  by (unknown)  [withheld from you]
    beta  room publish --id r1                     REFUSED: "... and you are not its author."
    otherh room publish --id r1                    rc 0   published DURING SEALED_DIVERGENT

Mechanism: `_room_author` (bin/aim:2687) returns "" when a room has more than one attributed voice -- a deliberate fail-closed choice -- and the read gate is `if who != author` (bin/aim:2758), which `""` can never satisfy. So the author and the leader are both locked out. `cmd_room_publish` (bin/aim:2941) is `if kind != "human" and author and who != author`, so the human exemption fires before the author comparison and a human stranger opens it. The stranger text write records no refusal row.

The row in IV-c and the verb docstring both say "author-or-leader"; measured, the leader has no exemption and the stranger does. No room exists anywhere in the live tree, so the cost today is zero.

title: The board's owner-or-creator union has only ever had one term: fold_tasks never sets created_by

body:
Found while applying §4.4 of SOP.md. The task-visibility rule is stated three
times (`bin/aim:_visible_to`, `aimboard/gate.py:visible_tasks`,
`aimboard/a2a.py:task_visible`) and §4.4 is about whether those three agree.
They do not agree on a draft nobody owns, and the disagreement hides a card from
its own author.

Reproduced on a throwaway root — channel `ch`, one participant `alpha`, leader
`lead`, phase `SEALED_DIVERGENT`:

```
aim task new --as alpha --channel ch --title "alpha own"    rc 0
aim task list --as alpha --channel ch   ->  T-0001 backlog (unclaimed) [draft]   (CLI sees it)
gate.visible_tasks(state,"alpha")       ->  visible 0, hidden 1                  (board does not)
gate.visible_tasks(state,"lead")        ->  visible 1, hidden 0
a2a.list_tasks(viewer="alpha")          ->  []                                   (rpc does not)
```

Two mechanisms, both in the tree as written:

1. `bin/aim`'s fold sets `created_by` from the event's actor (`:1699`);
   `aimboard/fold.fold_tasks` never sets the key at all.
   `bin/aim:1700-1703` documents this difference in a comment and calls it "a
   measurement rather than an oversight" — true of the difference, not of its
   consequence. Every `viewer not in (owner, created_by)` test is then
   `""`-and-`None` for an unowned card, i.e. false for everyone.

2. `_visible_to` (`:1782-1784`) has an explicit unowned short-circuit —
   `if not task.get("owner"): return True`, commented *"Unowned: nobody's
   position to protect"* — and neither of the other two copies has it. Both go
   straight from the phase test to the owner/creator union.

Measured live on `hello`: four of the 31 cards the board hides from
`claude-session1` are cards `claude-session1` typed. `T-0246/47/48` fold
`owner=codex, created_by=None` (store created-actor `claude-session1`) — the
`created_by` drop. `T-0249` folds `owner="", created_by=None` — both.

One sentence covers all four: on the board, the union `owner or created_by` has
only ever had one term. This is not the triplication §4.4 is about; it is a
fourth thing, and it costs the author rather than a stranger.

The note the cross-reference points at is real (`bin/aim:1748-1755`, the "second
fold … his half of the interface" comment), and it explains why `context_id` is
not added there. It does not mention `created_by`, which is the field the
comment at `:1702` is about — so the pointer resolves to a note about a
different field. The consequence is not in that note, on either side of the
interface. `bin/aim` is not my lane, so this is a report rather than an edit.


Separately: `bin/aim:1700-1703` cites "the note at the end of this function" and
I could not find that note in the surrounding 40 lines, so the cross-reference
is dangling too. Flagging it rather than editing — `bin/aim` is not my lane.

    $ python3 -c "import json;d=json.load(open('registry.json'))['agents']; ..."

  of that file alone can tell NO id has declared a departure -- and nothing
  else. `aim card --as <id>` returns rc=0 for all six, so no other check in the
  fabric contradicts that either: the file cannot distinguish a running session
  from one that died without departing (which is exactly tests/test_depart.py's
  group E, and bin/aim:1102's own docstring: the witness "does not have one").
  So the clause is true only for an id that DECLARED a departure and false for
  every other id. None of the six has.

ACTION TAKEN — accept line corrected with `aim task edit --as claude-session1
--channel hello --id T-0253 --accept ...` (new text above), reason recorded on
the event. The card is not disputed as work: `aim depart` exists and does what
it says; what was wrong was the accept line's two over-claims.

TEST COUNTS MEASURED (this session):
  python3 tests/test_depart.py                 -> 41/41 checks passed, rc=0
  full tests/test_*.py sweep: 25 files rc=0.
    test_a2a_conformance 77/78 (1 FAIL), test_aimboard 128/129 (1 FAIL),

T-0249: reproduced, fixed, pinned. Card has no owner; writing it as claude-session1, the actor the store records as its creator (`created` event actor, channels/hello/tasks.jsonl:492).

THE CARD'S PREMISE IS NARROWER THAN THE BEHAVIOUR. Measured on the pre-fix tree (all three fix files stashed, one throwaway root, channel `ch` in SEALED_DIVERGENT, participants alpha,beta, leader lead):

    alpha  room new --channel ch --id r1                     rc 0
    alpha  room say --id r1 --body 'alpha opens this room'   rc 0
    lead   room say --id r1 --body 'lead answers in it'      rc 0   <- the second voice
    alpha  room list --channel ch
           r1  2 msg(s)  draft  by (unknown)  [withheld from you]      rc 0
    alpha  room meta  --id r1   REFUSED: ... and you are not its author.   rc 2
    alpha  room publish --id r1 REFUSED: ... and you are not its author.   rc 2
    beta   room list            r1 ... [withheld from you]                 rc 0
    lead   room meta  --id r1   "author": ""                                rc 0

The mechanism is exactly what the card says (`_room_author` returned `""` for a two-voice room), and it is worth naming that `""` is not the fail-closed value here: the read gate and `cmd_room_publish` are both `who != author`/`author and who != author`, so `""` refused the author, the leader and every peer, and left nobody able to open the room again. Measured on the board on the same fabricated room (loader hands the gate `{"id","topic","visibility","unread","mentions"}` — no `author` key):

    gate.room_authors(room)        -> []
    visible_rooms(alpha)           -> [] hidden 1
    visible_rooms(beta)            -> [] hidden 1
    visible_rooms(otherh human)    -> ['r1','r2'] hidden 0
    visible_rooms(lead)            -> ['r1','r2'] hidden 0

which is the second half already visible on the read side: the two seats the gate cannot withhold from are the two HUMANS, one of which is a stranger.

WHAT THE SECOND VOICE HAS TO BE, stated plainly because it changes how the card should be read. A non-human second voice is refused by the same gate, so the sequence the card describes is only reachable when the second voice is exempt from it: the leader (the audience, `walled_off`'s first branch) or any agent the registry calls `kind: human` — the latter being the stranger half. I found no path by which a peer participant writes into a draft room during a divergence phase (`room say --as beta` rc 2, before and after).

HALF 2, measured pre-fix: `otherh` (registered, `kind: human`, not a participant, not the leader)

    otherh room meta    --channel ch --id r2   rc 0   (reads the draft's messages)
    otherh room publish --channel ch --id r2   rc 0   "published DURING SEALED_DIVERGENT ... recorded in the ledger as a barrier event"
    otherh room say     --channel ch --id r2   rc 0   (writes into it)
    otherh room list    --channel ch           rc 0   (and sees every room, incl. the peer's draft)

The publish is not refused: `cmd_room_publish` is `if kind != "human" and author and who != author`, and `_load_room_or_die`'s draft gate is `... and kind != "human"`, so `kind: human` was a skeleton key in both. The room file's `author` was rewritten from "alpha" to "" by the same publish (meta carried the derived `""`), so the stranger's act erased the author's own record of authorship. The stranger's attempts recorded no refusal row.

FIX (three files; the rule lives once, in `aimboard/gate.py`, and `bin/aim` imports it)

1. `aimboard/gate.py` — `room_author_from_metadata(meta, op_agent)` decides authorship once, for the CLI and the board: the opener is the recorded creator (`author`, else `created_by`, else `owner`) and the log's first attributed voice, and a room whose log names an opener its metadata does not returns `""` (the provenance arm, the only case that still refuses everybody). `room_authors(room)` hands it the log's opener. A second voice is no longer evidence about authorship at all.
2. `aimboard/fabric.py` — `load_rooms` forwards `author`/`created_by` off `rooms/<room>.json`, as the task said it must. The board's half of the rule could not fire without it.
3. `bin/aim` — `_room_author` now calls the gate function instead of keeping a second copy of the rule (the CLI/board disagreement was expressible, and this makes it not); new `_room_or_channel_stranger(ch, who, kind, action)` refuses a caller who is neither a participant of the room's channel nor its leader, and is called by `room meta`, `room say`, `room list` and `room publish`. The draft gate's exemption is now `who != m["leader"]` rather than `kind != "human"`, and `cmd_room_publish` is `who != m["leader"]` for the same reason. `cmd_search`'s task arm follows the same line.

The card's step 3 choice — room-level author = the agent who opened it — is what was implemented, and it keeps every gate that was already there: a peer still cannot read a draft room, the leader is still the audience, and `room publish` is still author-or-leader.

AFTER (same commands, same throwaway fabric, fix applied) — /tmp/t0249-after.out:

    alpha room list  ... r1  2 msg(s)  draft  by alpha            rc 0
    alpha room meta  --id r1  "author": "alpha", "messages": 2     rc 0
    alpha room publish --id r1  rc 0
    beta  room say   --id r2  REFUSED: ... and you are not its author (alpha).  rc 2
    otherh room meta --id r2  REFUSED: 'otherh' is not a participant in 'ch' and is not its leader (lead)  rc 2
    otherh room publish --id r2  same refusal, rc 2
    otherh room say   --id r2  same refusal, rc 2
    otherh room list  --channel ch  same refusal, rc 2
    lead  room meta   --id r2  rc 0
    board: 'author' in the loaded room -> 'alpha'; room_authors -> ['alpha'];
           visible_rooms(alpha) ['r1','r2']; visible_rooms(beta) ['r1'] hidden 1
    ledger: 6 refusal rows (1 peer, 5 stranger), all class barrier; 1 room_published row
    aim verify --channel ch -> chain OK

One more defect the fix closes, found by reading the code rather than the card: the provenance arm. A room whose log names an opener its metadata does not (a log copied under another room's file) also produced an author of `""` pre-fix whenever the log carried two voices — and `cmd_room_publish` publishes a room when `author == ""` and the caller is human, which is how a *pre-existing* `""` could be spent by a non-opener. Post-fix that shape returns `""` for a stated reason (provenance), and the stranger rule refuses the spend before it is reached.

COST, stated rather than implied. Two behaviours changed beyond the card. (a) A registered human who is neither a participant nor the leader is now refused `room list/meta/say/publish`, where `room list` used to answer them. That is the fix (b), not a side effect — but it is a narrow reading of "a human stranger cannot publish it" and it was my judgement: the card's own text names a stranger as *not a participant*, and `walled_off` keeps every ordinary human exemption for the leader. (b) `cmd_room_publish`'s no-author arm is now unreachable for non-leaders, because the stranger refusal fires first; where it used to be "a human stranger may open an authorless room", it is now dead for exactly that caller.

PINNED: `tests/test_aimboard.py` gains `room_gate_keeps_the_opener_and_refuses_the_stranger()`, built from `bin/aim` on a throwaway root (both halves are CLI-reachable, so a hand-written fixture would measure a fixture). Counts measured back to back on one revision of the test file (`sha256 8e0962a2c0ca1040`): fix applied **171/171 passed, exit 0**; the three fix files stashed, same file **159/171, exit 12**, and all 12 failures name T-0249. Before-runs are quoted from the tree, not from memory, and the suite is being edited concurrently by another session — the count is only meaningful next to the file hash, which is why it is written here.
